segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: This is how a person should regard us: as servants of Christ and stewards of God’s secrets.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now what is looked for in stewards is this: that one be found faithful.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But to me it matters very little that I should be examined by you or by any human court. In fact, I do not even examine myself.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For I am not aware of anything against myself, but I am not vindicated by that; the one who examines me is the Lord.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So do not judge anything before the time, until the Lord comes. He will bring to light the things hidden in darkness and disclose the purposes of hearts, and then each one’s praise will come from God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now, brothers and sisters, I have applied these things to myself and Apollos for your sake, so that in us you may learn the saying “Not beyond what is written,” so that none of you will be puffed up in favor of one against another.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For who sets you apart? What do you have that you did not receive? And if you did receive it, why do you boast as though you had not?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Already you have had your fill! Already you have become rich! Without us you have become kings! And I wish you really had become kings, so that we too might be kings with you!

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For it seems to me that God has put us apostles on display last, like people condemned to death, because we have become a spectacle to the world, to angels and to people.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: We are fools because of Christ, but you are sensible in Christ! We are weak, but you are strong! You are honored, but we are dishonored!

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: To this very hour we go hungry and thirsty, we are poorly clothed, we are beaten, we are homeless,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and we toil, working with our own hands. When we are insulted, we bless; when we are persecuted, we endure;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: when we are slandered, we answer kindly. We have become like the scum of the world, the dirt scraped off everything, right up to now.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I am not writing these things to shame you, but to warn you as my beloved children.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For even if you have ten thousand guardians in Christ, you do not have many fathers; for in Christ Jesus it was I who fathered you through the good news.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So I urge you: become imitators of me.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: This is why I have sent Timothy to you. He is my beloved and faithful child in the Lord, and he will remind you of my ways in Christ Jesus, just as I teach everywhere in every assembly.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But some have become puffed up, as though I were not coming to you.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But I will come to you soon, if the Lord wills, and I will find out not the talk of those who are puffed up but their power,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for the kingdom of God is not in talk but in power.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: What do you want? Shall I come to you with a rod, or with love and a spirit of gentleness?

notes.note: Most English versions keep “mysteries” here as an established technical term. In Jewish Greek of the period the word was the ordinary term for a secret, especially a plan of God that only he can disclose. “Mystery” now suggests a puzzle or something beyond understanding, whereas Paul means things God has made known and entrusted to his stewards to pass on. A steward was a household manager, often a slave, answerable to the master for what was placed in his charge.

The Greek says literally “a human day.” Paul appears to coin the phrase as a counterpart to “the day of the Lord,” the day when God judges (see 3:13): a day of reckoning set by human beings. Most translations render the sense as “human court” or “human judgment,” as here.

The traditional rendering is “justified,” and some versions have “acquitted.” The verb belongs to the same Greek word-family as “righteous” and “righteousness,” which English splits between two sets of words. Here the setting is a judicial examination, and Paul’s point is that a clear conscience is not itself a verdict in his favor; only the Lord’s finding counts.

The Greek plural is grammatically masculine but was the normal way to address a mixed group of men and women, as Paul’s assemblies were. “Brothers” alone would now be heard as excluding the women. Many modern translations make the same choice.

The verb elsewhere means to change the form or appearance of something. Here Paul seems to mean that he has cast his argument in terms of himself and Apollos as examples, perhaps tactfully avoiding naming the real offenders at Corinth. Some take it more simply as “I have used these figures of speech (farmers, builders, stewards) about myself and Apollos.”

notes.traditional: not to go beyond what is written
notes.note: The Greek is a clipped phrase with no verb, introduced as if it were a known slogan or proverb. Most interpreters take “what is written” to mean Scripture, perhaps the passages Paul has quoted in chapters 1–3 against human boasting. Others suggest a general maxim about keeping to the rules, and a few suspect the text is damaged. The exact reference is uncertain.

The word means a theater and, by extension, the show staged in it. Paul pictures the apostles as the condemned prisoners brought on last, either at the end of a victory procession or as the final act in the arena, where they were to die before the crowd. The audience here is the whole universe, heavenly and human.

Most translations have “wise.” The Greek word is not the one Paul uses for “wise” and “wisdom” throughout chapters 1–3; it means prudent, shrewd, having good sense. “Sensible” keeps the two words distinct. The tone is ironic, as in the rest of the verse.

notes.phrase: the scum of the world, the dirt scraped off everything
notes.traditional: the filth of the world, the offscouring of all things
notes.note: The two Greek nouns both mean the dirt removed when something is scoured or wiped clean, and both were used as terms of abuse for worthless people. Some scholars think they also carried the sense of a person sacrificed as a scapegoat to purify a city, but the evidence that this was a live meaning in Paul’s day is disputed. The second phrase could also be read “the dirt scraped off everyone.”

The word names a household slave who escorted a boy to and from school and supervised his conduct until he came of age. He was a minder and disciplinarian, not a teacher and certainly not a parent. Paul’s point is that the Corinthians may have any number of supervisors, but only one person brought them to life in Christ.

The traditional rendering is “gospel,” which is now a religious term or a book title. The Greek was an ordinary word for a public announcement of good news, used also of imperial proclamations. Many modern translations alternate between the two renderings.

“Church” is the near-universal rendering and readers know what it refers to. A first-century hearer knew the word as a civic gathering of citizens and as the Greek Old Testament’s term for Israel assembled before God. “Church” now suggests a building or an institution. “Assembly” is used throughout this translation so that the reader can see it is one Greek word.

Older versions have “meekness,” which now suggests weakness; the Greek does not. The word describes a person who is not harsh or self-assertive. “Gentleness” is the mainstream modern rendering. “Spirit” here is most likely a disposition, though some take it as a reference to God’s Spirit.

candidates.reason: The plural address to mixed congregations recurs in every letter, and versions split between “brothers” and “brothers and sisters,” so one policy is needed.
Usually rendered “wise,” which merges it with σοφός; it recurs in the Gospels (wise builder, wise as serpents, wise virgins) and in Paul, and needs one rendering distinct from σοφός.

It occurs ten times in 1 Corinthians and in Luke–Acts for judicial inquiry, and versions vary among “judge,” “examine,” “discern,” and “call to account,” obscuring the link with κρίνω and with 2:14–15.
It occurs here and in Galatians 3:24–25, where “tutor,” “schoolmaster,” “guardian,” and “disciplinarian” all compete and the choice shapes how the Law’s role is read.
It recurs in Luke’s parables, Paul, Titus, and 1 Peter, where “steward” and “manager” compete; “steward” is slightly archaic but “manager” loses the household setting.
